entry.title: A national body runs the analytics and the university runs the support (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Jisc reports that the University of Northampton has chosen its learning analytics service for the whole institution, replacing two separate systems with one, and will extend access to all students from September with full rollout at the start of the 2026 to 2027 academic year. The service combines attendance monitoring, engagement dashboards, reporting and analytics, case management and a student app in one environment. Jisc names Abertay, Bournemouth, City St George's University of London, Salford, South Wales and Suffolk among the other United Kingdom providers already using it.

Why it matters here: PASS is building models from Wits data with the University's Business Intelligence Services, so the interesting part here is the division of labour: a national body supplies the analytics platform while each university keeps the case management and the intervention. It is a live example of the shared-service option Wits could weigh against building everything in house.

Jisc, news item, 20 August 2026 · Announcement from Jisc, the United Kingdom's national body for digital services in tertiary education

entry.title: Seven hundred students across three subjects say what escape rooms actually taught them (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Four researchers at the University of Auckland and Bond University surveyed students and educators about escape room games used in three distinct degree programmes at one large university, and received 708 student responses and eight educator responses. The quantitative answers were analysed descriptively and the written answers by thematic analysis. Students and educators in medical sciences, biological sciences and education all reported rich and many-sided learning, and the authors found that escape rooms promoted similar transferable skills and motivations whatever the disciplinary context. Their recommendation is to use escape rooms sparingly.

Why it matters here: It gives the Wits study a survey design and a sample size to aim at, and its finding that the gains hold across very different disciplines is an argument for trying an escape room in metallurgy at all. The advice to use them sparingly is a useful check on how often a gamified activity should appear in one course.

Kam, M., Clune, M., Jowsey, T. and Singleton, R., Higher Education Research and Development, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, hybrid open access under CC BY-NC-ND

entry.title: Thirty-three thousand Assam student records, and a model that explains why it flagged you (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Six authors led from Dibrugarh University in Assam analysed 33,627 student records from colleges affiliated to the university, covering students admitted in 2023 and 39 academic and demographic attributes. They compared regression and classification methods and then used explainable artificial intelligence techniques, including SHAP and LIME, to show which features drove each prediction. Logistic regression identified at-risk students with 98.43 per cent accuracy, 99.08 per cent precision and 97.86 per cent recall, and the most influential features were total credit points and overall semester marks, with raised dropout risk below 200 marks and 50 credit points.

Why it matters here: PASS will have to justify to staff and to students why a model flagged a particular person, and this study shows the explanation layer being built in from the start rather than added afterwards. The scale, drawn from affiliated colleges rather than one campus, is also close to the kind of multi-site data a South African faculty would need to pool.

Paul, R., Sarker, S., El Aouifi, H., Hussain, S., Baruah, A. K. and Gaftandzhieva, S., Frontiers in Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A report puts a price on Africa's outbound students and asks who gains (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
This report frames outbound African student mobility as a continental economic question rather than an individual opportunity. It states that more than 460,000 African students leave the continent each year for higher education abroad, at an estimated annual loss of 2.5 billion United States dollars in tuition, innovation and forgone opportunity, and that while 54 per cent of those students are scholarship funded only 18 per cent return. It argues that African countries together spend more on overseas tuition than 25 countries spend on their entire education budgets, and estimates a 500 million dollar annual reinvestment if a quarter of mobile students stayed through hybrid programmes.

Why it matters here: The Wits and Aix-Marseille project sends people out and brings people in, and this is the sharpest available statement of the risk on the outbound side, that mobility can shade into permanent departure. Reading it alongside the project's design is a way of asking what keeps a returning candidate in place, and its figures are a useful counterweight to the celebratory register of most mobility reporting, though they come from a private research group rather than a peer-reviewed source.

Ekanem, K., African Student Mobility Report 2025, Mo-Research Strategy Group, published on Zenodo · Independent research report, openly available on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, not peer reviewed

entry.title: A mining and metallurgy school built its own simulation game for its own exploration course (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Three staff at the School of Mining and Metallurgical Engineering of the National Technical University of Athens used a design-based research approach to build and evaluate an educational simulation game for probabilistic and spatial reasoning in mineral exploration. The application generates random scenarios in which players direct exploration decisions and end by estimating ore reserves. The game has been adopted as a teaching tool in the course Introduction to Mineral Exploration at the school, and the paper reports game analytics together with a qualitative evaluation drawn from three workshops at higher education institutions in Greece.

Why it matters here: This is the closest published parallel to the Wits study: a mining and metallurgical engineering school designing a game for its own curriculum rather than borrowing one from elsewhere. The design-based research method, and the pairing of game analytics with qualitative evaluation, offer a template for the co-design workshops and classroom observation already planned at Wits.

Valakas, G., Sideri, D. and Modis, K., J, volume 8, article 38, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access under CC BY 4.0

entry.title: An Erasmus Mundus master on education, migration and diversity keeps multilingualism as a core module (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
EDU_MIG is an Erasmus Mundus master in Education, Migration and Diversity that began taking students in 2025, coordinated by the University of Education Schwäbisch Gmünd with the University of Gävle and the University of Calabria. It offers 25 places a year, a majority of them carrying Erasmus Mundus scholarships that cover tuition, health insurance and a monthly allowance, over two years with mobility between the partner countries. The curriculum is built on three core strands, Migration and Interculturality, Multilingualism, and Educational Sciences, and the network of academic and professional partners runs across Germany, Sweden, Italy, Türkiye and Benin, where students can take internships.

Why it matters here: The Wits and Aix-Marseille project moves master's students in bilingual teaching and academics working on multilingualism, and this is a fully built European programme with multilingualism as a named module and an African partner already inside the consortium. It is worth reading both as a curriculum model for the bilingual teaching strand and as a possible route by which a Wits colleague could join a Mundus consortium later.

EDU_MIG consortium, programme website, first cohort from 2025 · Official programme website of a consortium funded by the European Union under Erasmus Mundus

entry.title: Forty-nine engineering students played a workplace game for four weeks and their empathy scores rose (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Three researchers, two of them at Universiti Malaysia Sarawak, tested a serious game called HR Toxic Workplace with 49 engineering project management students at a Malaysian public university. The students played in weekly sessions across four weeks, and empathy was measured before and after with Davis's Interpersonal Reactivity Index, which covers perspective taking, empathic concern, personal distress and fantasy. The study reports significant improvements in empathy, strongest in perspective taking and personal distress, and collected qualitative data alongside the scores.

Why it matters here: The Wits study asks what teaching and assessment beyond the exam can reach, and this is a worked example of a game measuring something an exam cannot: a published instrument, a four-week schedule and a cohort of 49, all small enough to run inside a single metallurgical engineering course.

Techanamurthy, U., Chuah, K.-M. and Yee, I., Australasian Journal of Engineering Education, volume 30, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Colombia costed its national dropout early-warning system and found it paid for itself (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The Colombian Ministry of Education launched SPADIES, the System for the Prevention and Analysis of School Dropouts in Higher Education Institutions, in 2004 to help institutions collect, analyse and visualise student data, prevent dropout and re-engage students who had already left. Using a differences-in-differences design, the study finds SPADIES lowered dropout probability by 0.7 percentage points, raised on-time graduation by 0.6 points and overall graduation by 0.4 points. The author notes that 0.7 percentage points is roughly 14,000 students, and that the system cost 4.9 million United States dollars between 2005 and 2017 at 2025 prices, about 350 dollars for each student who did not drop out.

Why it matters here: PASS is being built one faculty at a time, and this is what the same idea looks like after twenty years at national scale, with a causal design and a price tag attached. The cost per student retained is the figure a Wits business case would need, and the modest effect size is a realistic expectation to set against the accuracy numbers that prediction papers usually report.

Herrera-Prada, L. O., International Journal of Educational Development, volume 116, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, subscription access

entry.title: Two hundred and fifty mobilities between Britain, Uganda and Kenya, and a survey to find out what they were worth (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Nottingham Trent University reports that its Erasmus+ International Credit Mobility programme ran in two phases, 2018 to 2021 and 2021 to 2023, and enabled over 250 transnational mobilities between the United Kingdom, Uganda and Kenya. The first phase paired NTU with Makerere University in public health for research development, capacity building and knowledge exchange among staff and undergraduate, master's and doctoral students; the second widened to nursing, microbiology and environmental sciences, and to Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology and Mount Kenya University on a 36 month grant of 136,360 euros. Participants took part in research training, writing retreats, summer schools and conference presentations, and the university has since run an ethics-approved survey of NTU and Makerere participants to assess what the mobilities changed.

Why it matters here: This is the nearest completed model of what the Wits and Aix-Marseille project is starting: a multi-year, two-direction partnership between a European and African university running across degree levels and staff. The detail worth borrowing is the evaluation, an ethics-approved survey of participants after the fact, which is exactly the evidence a 36 month project should be gathering from its first cohort rather than at the end.

Nottingham Trent University, Eastern Africa Centre project page, updated July 2024 · Project page of the host university, naming partners, funding and leads

entry.title: Wits signs the CIVIS Africa Charter and confirms its first Erasmus Mundus joint master's bid at the Casablanca forum (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
At the first African-European CIVIS Forum for Research and Education, held in Casablanca, Morocco, from 25 to 27 March 2026, the University of the Witwatersrand signed the Africa Charter for Transformative Research Collaborations, which sets out ten principles on power imbalances in global knowledge production and six policy aspirations for institutional change. Wits also confirmed it will lead its first African application to the European Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's programme, on polycrisis studies, and reported CIVIS staff and student mobility already running through its TRACEE master's programme and Blended Intensive Programmes.

Why it matters here: This project's own academic lead at Wits, Professor Emmanuel Ojo, is named in the same report as co-developing a CIVIS doctoral micro-credential on artificial intelligence and research with partner universities in Madrid, Rome, Athens and Glasgow, showing an existing staff mobility channel and a joint credentialing model the Aix-Marseille partnership can draw on, while the Africa Charter's principles on power imbalance are a direct check for the project's own design.

University of the Witwatersrand, September 2026 · Institutional news article, University of the Witwatersrand

entry.title: A Trivial-Pursuit-style board game for antennas and propagation is linked to higher exam grades over three years at a Madrid university (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Two lecturers at Universidad San Pablo-CEU and Universidad Autonoma de Madrid built a Trivial-Pursuit-style board game with 270 custom question cards and wildcards for the undergraduate 'Radiocommunications' course, commonly known elsewhere as Antennas and Propagation, and ran it once each December from 2023 to 2025. Comparing 47 students who played against 13 who did not, a Welch's t-test found players averaged 5.35 out of 10 against 2.85 for non-players (p = 0.0016, Cohen's d = 1.05), and an anonymous eleven-item survey rated the activity above 4.2 out of 5 on every question.

Why it matters here: The paper supplies a ready-made template, a question-card board game keyed to course syllabus units and run once a semester before exams, plus a rare quantitative grade comparison using Welch's t-test and Cohen's d that the Wits AHEAD project could adapt for its own crystallography or phase-transformation board game.

Domenech, A.S. and Alex-Amor, A., arXiv preprint, 2026 · Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, open access via arXiv

entry.title: Random forest model identifies Peruvian university dropout risk with 87 percent accuracy (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Four Peruvian university researchers built a predictive framework using the knowledge discovery in databases (KDD) methodology of selection, preprocessing, transformation, data mining and interpretation to flag Latin American university students at risk of dropping out. Their random forest model reached 87% accuracy, 86% precision, 85% recall, an F1-score of 85% and a ROC AUC of 0.91, outperforming the other approaches they tested, and the authors recommend it be adopted by universities for early identification of at-risk students.

Why it matters here: Provides PASS with a recent, fully open-access Latin American benchmark for a transparent tree-based classifier reaching strong accuracy on dropout risk, a useful comparison point for the models PASS will validate on Wits School of Education data, and evidence that KDD-style data pipelines translate well across university contexts.

Andrade-Arenas, Rubio Paucar, Giraldo Retuerto and Yactayo-Arias, IAES International Journal of Artificial Intelligence (IJ-AI), 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Propensity score analysis shows a university scholarship cuts dropout odds by 40 percent (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Two San Diego State University statisticians compared five predictive models, lasso regression, a generalised additive model, random forest, XGBoost and a neural network, on 3,400 records of students at Portugal's Polytechnic Institute of Portalegre enrolled between 2008/09 and 2018/19. XGBoost reached the best F1-score of 0.904, with 88.2% accuracy and 94.7% precision, and random forest reached the best area under the curve at 0.935; a propensity score matching analysis then found that receiving a scholarship reduced the odds of dropping out by nearly 40%, equivalent to a 22.2 percentage point drop in dropout probability.

Why it matters here: Goes beyond prediction to intervention evidence, exactly PASS's next step of co-creating interventions with the University's Business Intelligence Services: it demonstrates a rigorous, quasi-experimental method, propensity score matching, for testing whether a specific support measure, a scholarship, actually reduces dropout once confounders are controlled for.

Romero and Liao, PLoS ONE, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Randomised trial finds human judgement still matters inside Georgia State's advising algorithm (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers from Princeton University, Columbia Business School and Georgia State University's own advising team analysed a randomised controlled trial of Georgia State's algorithm-assisted advising programme. They found that roughly two out of three interventions advisers made in the treatment arm were expertly targeted using context the algorithm did not have, such as students' personal circumstances, financial factors and engagement, drawn from advisers' own notes, and that different advising styles were associated with different graduation rates.

Why it matters here: A direct empirical caution for PASS as it moves from prediction to co-created interventions with Business Intelligence Services and advisers: it shows that even a mature, long-running algorithmic advising system still depends on advisers' contextual judgement, supporting a human-in-the-loop design rather than a fully automated one.

Schechtman, Brandon, Stafford, Li and Liu, arXiv preprint, 2025 (accepted for ACM EAAMO 2025) · Working paper (arXiv preprint), co-authored with Georgia State University's own advising staff, accepted for the ACM Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms and Optimization (EAAMO) 2025 conference

entry.title: A Southeast Asian policy brief sets out how ten countries could build a shared framework for teacher exchange and mutual recognition (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A 2025 policy brief from the ASEAN Secretariat, written by a researcher at the University of the Philippines and based on focus groups and key informant interviews, found that Southeast Asian nations have used mutual recognition arrangements since 2005 in seven professional sectors, from engineering to accountancy, but never for teaching. It reported that about a quarter of pre-primary teachers and almost a tenth of primary teachers in the region lacked nationally recognised qualifications, and it recommended an ASEAN teacher exchange scheme, a regional coordination body, and visa, language and short-term training support for mobile teachers.

Why it matters here: A comparative case from outside Europe: its focus on mutual recognition of qualifications and on visa, language and pre-departure training support for mobile teachers names the same practical hurdles that the Wits and Aix-Marseille project must plan for as it moves students and staff between two different national qualification systems, and its call for a dedicated regional coordination body is a model the project's own administrative strand could test.

Dr Ethel Agnes Pascua-Valenzuela, ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community Policy Brief No. 22, 2025 · Intergovernmental policy brief, ASEAN Secretariat, open access

entry.title: A scoping review of virtual exchange research in teacher education finds outcomes depend on educator effort and institutional backing (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A scoping review by researchers at the University of Education Freiburg, published in the Center for Educational Policy Studies Journal in March 2025, examined research published between 2020 and 2023 on virtual exchange in teacher education, covering how such exchanges are planned, implemented and evaluated. It found virtual exchange to be a multifaceted field with multiple aims and impacts whose success depends heavily on educator effort, institutional support and student participation, and called for future research to move beyond language teacher education and to combine different study scales.

Why it matters here: Evidence and a ready-made literature map for the project's virtual and blended mobility strand: it can guide how the Wits and Aix-Marseille partnership designs, resources and evaluates any online or blended components alongside physical exchange, and its finding that outcomes hinge on institutional support is a direct planning point for both partners.

Claudia Ingrisch-Rupp and Vasileios Symeonidis, Center for Educational Policy Studies Journal, Vol. 15 No. 1, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Eleven experts set out how digital escape games should be designed for STEM courses, engineering education included (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Two researchers at the University of Education Karlsruhe and Karlsruhe University of Applied Sciences interviewed eleven experts, including educators, students, software engineers and industry professionals, on how digital escape games should be designed for STEM university courses. Qualitative content analysis found that game design must follow the learning objectives, with storytelling, varied puzzles, rising difficulty and immediate feedback as essential elements, while timers, competition and rewards divided expert opinion. One of the studies the authors reviewed had already tested a digital escape game in engineering education with 31 students.

Why it matters here: Escape rooms are named directly in the project's own search brief, and this study offers concrete design guidance, on feedback, puzzle progression and the risks of timers and competition, that could shape an escape-room-style assessment activity built around crystallography or phase transformations.

Gruber, M. and Fassbender, S., Frontiers in Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A three-year study of a Mexican logistics-engineering game platform links it to stronger self-directed learning skills (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Tecnologico de Monterrey and Aston University deployed LOST, a serious-game platform, in an undergraduate logistics engineering course in Mexico and tracked students' self-directed learning with an adapted Fisher, King and Tague scale across academic terms from 2017 to 2020. They report significant gains across five self-directed learning factors, including self-management, openness to learning opportunities and initiative and independence in learning, alongside a supporting review of 34 Scopus-indexed studies on game-based learning in complex scenarios.

Why it matters here: This three-year, Latin American study shows how a validated self-directed learning scale can be layered onto a gamified engineering course to track effects beyond exam grades, a method the Wits AHEAD project's own surveys, interviews and classroom observation could borrow when evaluating its board-game and digital-game interventions.

Pacheco-Velazquez, E., Rodes, V. and Salinas-Navarro, D., Journal of Technology and Science Education, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: South Africa in Erasmus+: 2,746 outbound and 1,879 inbound mobilities in the last programme, and 600 more student places to Europe from the 2022 selections (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The DHET's international scholarships portal records South Africa's participation in Erasmus+ since 2014 across all the components open to partner countries. Under the 2014 to 2020 programme, International Credit Mobility took 2,746 students and staff from South Africa to Europe and brought 1,879 from Europe to South Africa; 78 South African students won full Erasmus Mundus Joint Master scholarships, 29 capacity-building projects ran with four coordinated by South African institutions, and six Jean Monnet projects and one network were implemented. From the 2022 selections of the 2021 to 2027 programme, the page lists 461 staff mobilities to Europe and 416 from Europe to South Africa, 600 student mobilities to Europe and 128 into South Africa, three new capacity-building projects, ten instances of TVET capacity-building participation and five instances in two virtual exchange projects.

Why it matters here: The national picture into which the Aix-Marseille partnership fits: these figures show that the Wits mobilities are part of an established South African flow with a home department that tracks it, which matters for reporting, for Wits International's dealings with DHET, and for arguing that teacher education deserves a larger share.

Department of Higher Education and Training, International Scholarships portal, Erasmus+ Programme page (consulted 18 September 2026) · Official page of a national government department

entry.title: What the partner already runs: INSPE Aix-Marseille's student mobility page, from Erasmus+ semesters to CIVIS schools and teaching placements abroad (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The Institute of Teaching and Education (INSPE) at Aix-Marseille Université sets out the mobility routes open to its trainee teachers. Erasmus+ study periods last from three to twelve months per study cycle at eleven partner universities in Germany, Belgium, Denmark, Spain, Greece, the Netherlands and Switzerland, with credits validated on return; CIVIS supports study visits to alliance partners, and CIVIS schools offer one- to three-week intensive courses with practical work. Short formats include the International Education Week summer school at Tübingen, taught in English, and a Franco-German musical education exchange with Universität Hamburg. Placement mobility covers Erasmus+ teaching internships of two to twelve months and France Éducation International language-assistant posts of four to twelve months, with grants arranged through the international mobility manager.

Why it matters here: This is the machinery the Wits School of Education will plug into: INSPE already sends and receives trainee teachers on semester exchanges and short CIVIS formats, so the KA171 mobilities can copy its credit validation, its short-course model and its mobility-manager role rather than inventing them.

INSPE Aix-Marseille, International, Student mobility page (consulted 18 September 2026) · Official page of the partner institution

entry.title: Predicting late postgraduate graduation at Makerere: 500 students, 71% finishing late, and a simple logistic model that matches the ensembles (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A retrospective modelling study used anonymised administrative records of 500 postgraduate students registered at Makerere University between 2017 and 2023, of whom 29% graduated on time and 71% late. Random forest, XGBoost, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and a stacking ensemble all reached similar accuracy of about 94% to 95% and ROC-AUC between 0.94 and 0.95, with logistic regression numerically highest at 0.950 and no statistically meaningful differences between classifiers. Being employed and older age at admission were associated with delayed graduation, while a higher undergraduate grade point average reduced the likelihood of late completion; the authors argue that interpretable models can match complex ensembles on structured educational data.

Why it matters here: A direct African precedent for PASS on the postgraduate side: the same outcome (timely completion), the same reliance on anonymised institutional records, and a finding that a transparent model performs as well as ensembles, which supports the project's aim of models that advisers and Business Intelligence Services can explain.

Lubelenga, Kivunike, Chongomweru and Ahishakiye, Discover Artificial Intelligence, volume 6, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY)

entry.title: Twenty-two studies, one large effect: a Ghanaian meta-analysis of gamification in higher education finds engineering among the disciplines that gain most (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Four researchers at the University of Cape Coast pooled 22 independent studies of gamification in higher education in a random-effects meta-analysis. They report a large overall effect on learning outcomes (Cohen's d = 1.12, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.83) with very high heterogeneity (I squared = 98.84%). Moderator analyses found larger effects in business, mathematics and engineering, in face-to-face settings, over moderate durations of three to six months, and where the design followed a structured framework such as the Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics model; competitive designs outperformed narrative ones, and deep learning and academic performance gained more than engagement.

Why it matters here: An African synthesis the Wits study can cite for its rationale and design: it argues for a structured game design, a semester-length intervention and outcome measures that go beyond engagement, and its finding that engineering shows larger effects gives the metallurgy classroom a benchmark to test against.

Gyedu, Partey, Boafo and Agbo, Sage Open, volume 16, issue 1, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC)

entry.title: Fifty-five educators on what Erasmus staff exchange did for them: leadership, intercultural competence and the barriers that keep others at home (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A qualitative study at Transylvania University of Brașov drew on in-depth interviews with 55 educators from European and non-European countries who had taken part in Erasmus staff exchange, tracing how short-term mobility reshaped their professional practice, career paths and engagement with their institutions. Participants reported gains in intercultural competence, global awareness and pedagogical innovation, and described a renewed sense of purpose and an expanded leadership identity on return. The authors also record persistent barriers, including financial constraints, gaps in language proficiency and uneven institutional support, and argue that unless these are addressed Erasmus will serve the already advantaged rather than transform education systems.

Why it matters here: Evidence for the staff strand of the Wits and Aix-Marseille project: it suggests what to ask returning academics and administrators in the project's own evaluation, and its warning about language and institutional support speaks directly to a partnership working across English and French.

Ivasciuc, Marinescu and Ispas, Education Sciences, volume 15, issue 6, article 712, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY)

entry.title: Inside the black box: student-success predictions are less accurate for racially minoritised students, and the usual bias fixes do not close the gap (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Using nationally representative data from the Education Longitudinal Study of 2002 and several machine learning approaches, the authors tested how accurately models built on commonly used features predict college success for different racialised groups. The models were less accurate for racially minoritised students, which the authors read as algorithmic bias inherited from historical data that captures societal injustice, including racism. They then applied leading bias-mitigation techniques and found them generally ineffective at removing the disparities in prediction outcomes and accuracy between groups. The American Educational Research Association named the paper the most outstanding article published in its journals in 2025.

Why it matters here: A caution PASS must design against from the start: accuracy has to be reported by group, not just overall, and the Wits models, trained on a South African student body with its own historical inequities, cannot assume that off-the-shelf fairness adjustments will fix disparities that the data carry.

Gándara, Anahideh, Ison and Picchiarini, AERA Open, volume 10, 2024; winner of AERA's 2025 Palmer O. Johnson Memorial Award · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC); AERA award for the most outstanding article in an AERA journal

entry.title: 11,698 first-year students and 69 variables: a random-forest early-warning model in Türkiye reaches 90.2% accuracy once the first-semester average is known (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers from three Istanbul universities and a bank's business intelligence department built an early-warning system that classifies first-year undergraduates as likely to succeed or fail by the end of the year. The dataset covered 11,698 first-year students and 69 input variables; naive Bayes, decision tree and random forest models were compared, and random forest performed best with 90.2% accuracy. Models that included the autumn-semester grade point average performed dramatically better, and the student's programme and university placement examination score were the next most important variables. The authors propose acting on the predictions from the second week of the spring semester so that support reaches students before attrition occurs.

Why it matters here: A useful comparison for the Wits School of Education data: the finding that the first-semester average dominates suggests PASS should test how early a reliable flag can be raised, and the joint authorship with a business intelligence unit mirrors the project's planned work with Wits Business Intelligence Services.

Çırak, Akıllı and Ekinci, Higher Education Quarterly, volume 78, issue 4, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Wiley)

entry.title: Crystal Vision: a virtual-reality game for crystallography lifts quiz scores by 9% and cuts completion time by 19% for 84 undergraduates (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A team spanning civil, electrical and computer engineering, information sciences and computer science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign built Crystal Vision, a virtual-reality game that teaches basic crystallographic concepts to undergraduates. Systematic testing with 84 students showed a 9% rise in quiz scores (from 7.45 to 8.12 out of 10) and a 19% fall in quiz completion time (from 7.39 to 5.98 minutes) after the VR intervention. Students who felt comfortable moving through the game agreed more strongly with most survey statements, which the authors read as evidence that user comfort inside a VR game shapes learning outcomes.

Why it matters here: The closest published match to the Wits study's content: crystal structures are exactly the spatial concepts the metallurgy cohort struggles with, and this paper offers a pre-test and post-test design with timed quizzes and a comfort measure that the project could adapt for its digital game arm.

Bejjarapu, Chen, Xu, Shaffer and Garg, Journal of Chemical Education, volume 101, issue 3, pages 973 to 983, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article (American Chemical Society)

entry.title: Escape our Lab: a materials-science and crystallography escape room built inside a real teaching laboratory, with the puzzle sheets published (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
The Institute of Materials Science at TU Bergakademie Freiberg turned part of a laboratory and an adjoining seminar room into an escape room on materials science and crystallography, first run in 2019 as part of a campaign to attract students to the field. Fourteen puzzles across four rooms use real equipment such as furnaces, hardness testers, single-crystal diffraction patterns and an overhead projector, in a 60-minute short variant or a 90-minute long one; the set-up takes about an hour and the laboratory can be restored for regular teaching. The paper reports that more than 50 groups, mainly secondary pupils but also undergraduates and teachers, had played, that every puzzle can be solved without the game master's help, and that a debriefing linking each puzzle to the science is the most important step; the to-do list, hints and participation certificate are published as supporting information.

Why it matters here: A ready-made template for a low-cost, analogue game in the Wits metallurgy laboratories: the puzzles already cover diffraction and hardness, the materials are open, and the authors' observations on team dynamics and debriefing are useful design notes for the project's co-design workshops.

Schimpf, Lachmann, Wetzel, Fischer, Leineweber and Rafaja, Journal of Applied Crystallography, volume 56, pages 1544 to 1556, 2023 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY), with supporting information

entry.title: How Erasmus+ KA171 mobility works: the rules this project runs under (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The Erasmus+ Programme Guide sets the rules for mobility projects for higher education students and staff. Projects supported by external policy funds, the strand this partnership falls under, run for 24 or 36 months, cover every study cycle from short cycle to doctoral, and allow blended mobility that combines a physical stay with a virtual component. Regional rules apply: for Sub-Saharan Africa at least 35% of the budget must go to mobility with the region's least developed countries and no more than 8% to any single country. Partner institutions outside the Programme countries cannot sign the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education but must respect its principles, so fair and transparent selection, recognition of learning outcomes and support for participants have to be made explicit in the inter-institutional agreement.

Why it matters here: The rulebook for this project: the 36-month duration, the doctoral and blended mobility options, and the requirement that selection and recognition be spelt out in the inter-institutional agreement all come from here, which is why the Wits side's first task is that agreement.

European Commission, Erasmus+ Programme Guide, Part B, Key Action 1, mobility projects for higher education students and staff (version consulted 16 September 2026) · Official programme guide of the European Commission

entry.title: CIVIS asks Europe to treat academic mobility from Africa as a visa priority (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
CIVIS, the European University Alliance to which Aix-Marseille University belongs and which has African member institutions, has published a position paper on visas for Africa-Europe academic mobility. Drawing on its own surveys, it reports that African applicants face long waiting times, difficulty getting appointments, high costs, long journeys to consulates and heavy documentation, which lead to delayed or cancelled exchanges. It welcomes the European Commission's moves to modernise visa policy and asks for three additions: academic mobility as a priority category with longer-validity, multiple-entry visas; simplified procedures extended to short academic stays such as conferences and research visits; and strategic priority for Africa, with more consular capacity and faster processing.

Why it matters here: The practical risk this project must plan for: a Wits student or colleague holding an Erasmus+ grant still needs a French visa in time, so nomination windows and consulate lead times belong in the mobility calendar from the start, and the CIVIS position gives the partnership a policy argument to cite.

CIVIS position paper and newsroom, 9 September 2026 · Position paper of a European University Alliance, drawing on its own member surveys

entry.title: From risk score to recommended action: prescriptive dropout analytics for 2,500 foundation-programme entrants in Ecuador (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Escuela Superior Politécnica del Litoral (ESPOL) in Guayaquil built a prescriptive analytics pipeline for a computing-oriented bachelor's programme, tracking 2,500 students who entered its foundation programme between 2020 and 2024, of whom 9.1% (228) dropped out. A Random Forest classifier using 58 features drawn from foundation-stage academic, socioeconomic and connectivity data reached a ROC-AUC of 0.95 to 0.97; k-means clustering split students into three profiles with observed dropout of 0.6% (high-resource), 5.7% (intermediate) and 25.7% (vulnerable), and the authors added SHAP explanations and counterfactual recourse tools (DiCE, CARLA, Alibi) to turn each score into a specific recommended action.

Why it matters here: Goes a step beyond prediction to prescription, the direction PASS itself wants to take once its own risk model is validated: a worked example of turning a risk score into an explainable, student-specific recommendation, and a profile-based reading of risk (by resource level, not just a single score) that the Emory-Wits team could test against its own Wits School of Education data.

Quijije-Castro, Peláez and colleagues, Frontiers in Education 11 (2026), open access · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Gradient boosting and 32 advisers: a deployed early-warning system evaluated for usability, not just accuracy (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at ISI Bali and Universitas Sains dan Teknologi Komputer, Semarang, built and deployed a web-based early-warning system on 1,240 student records from 2021 to 2024, combining institutional records with Moodle behavioural data such as weekly login frequency and assignment submission timing. A Gradient Boosting model, chosen after comparing four algorithms with stratified ten-fold cross-validation and SMOTE class balancing, reached 89.1% accuracy, an F1-score of 0.850 and an AUC-ROC of 0.931; 32 academic advisers then rated the deployed system on the System Usability Scale at a mean of 78.4, above-average usability.

Why it matters here: Most early-warning papers in this feed stop at model accuracy; this one also asks whether the advisers who receive the alerts find the system usable, a question PASS will face once its own model reaches Wits School of Education advisers, and the login-frequency and submission-timing predictors are simple LMS signals the project could test early.

Handayani and Priyadi, Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Information Technology (2026) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: An Edge-AI gamification framework claims a 51% engagement gain in engineering classrooms (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Chitkara University Institute of Engineering and Technology, Punjab, and Graphic Era Deemed to be University proposed an Edge-AI gamification framework that pairs edge computing with an "Edge-AI Gamification Optimizer" algorithm to deliver real-time, personalised educational games, quizzes and competitive learning tools in engineering courses. Comparing the framework against traditional teaching, the authors report a rise of nearly 51% in student engagement, 30.7% in performance and a fall of 57% in cognitive load, alongside gains in knowledge retention, collaborative learning and motivation.

Why it matters here: The clearest fit yet for the "AI-mediated" half of this project's brief: a framework built specifically to personalise gamification in real time using AI, for the Wits team to weigh against its own plans for AI-generated or AI-mediated games, though the size of the reported gains argues for reading the framework, not yet an independent replication, with appropriate caution.

Singh and Singh, Computer Applications in Engineering Education (2025) · Peer-reviewed journal article; large reported effect sizes not yet independently replicated

entry.title: Kahoot versus paper: a controlled quiz comparison in a mechanics course at Pakistan's National University of Sciences and Technology (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
At the School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, National University of Sciences and Technology, Islamabad, 64 engineering students volunteered for a controlled comparison of the Kahoot quiz app against paper-based quizzes across mechanics units on buckling and beam deflection, 32 students to a group. Each unit opened with a Kahoot warm-up and closed with a unit quiz; Likert-scale surveys and z-tests and t-tests found motivation, engagement, fun, concentration and learning outcomes were all significantly higher in the Kahoot group than the paper-based group.

Why it matters here: A controlled, same-topic comparison (game app against paper) rather than the single-arm surveys most gamification cases in this feed report; useful evidence for the CheMet team's own comparison of gamified and non-gamified sections, and confirmation that even a low-cost quiz app, not a bespoke game, produces a measurable gap.

Lashari, Fiayaz, Lashari, Khan, Sultana and Afzal, Computer Applications in Engineering Education 32(2), 2024 (published online 2023) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: 143,326 anonymised records, seven cohorts: an open dropout-prediction dataset from Tecnologico de Monterrey (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Tecnologico de Monterrey released a curated, non-identifiable dataset of 50 variables across 143,326 records covering 121,584 high school and undergraduate students from seven admission cohorts, August to December 2014 to 2020, spanning two educational models. The variables cover sociodemographic and academic information alongside institution-specific measures such as student life, and the dataset was built specifically so other researchers can train and compare dropout-prediction models.

Why it matters here: An open, ready-to-use dataset at a scale the PASS team is unlikely to match from Wits School of Education records alone; a natural benchmark for testing whether models built on South African data generalise, or a training set to trial methods on before running them on the School's own anonymised data.

Alvarado-Uribe, Mejía-Almada, Herrera, Molontay, Hilliger, Hegde, Montemayor Gallegos, Díaz and Ceballos, Data 7(9), 119 (2022), open access, CC BY · Peer-reviewed data descriptor, open access, CC BY

entry.title: A vector-operations video game built in Unity lifts marks in a first-year engineering science course (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Universidad de Ibagué's GESE research group built a Unity video game to teach vector addition, the dot product and the cross product to first-year engineering students in a basic sciences course. Forty of the roughly 100 students on the course played the game across a semester; a quantitative, non-experimental evaluation compared conceptual test scores before and after play and found an attitudinal improvement towards the course and a significant rise in academic performance, with final marks of 56.53% at 3.0 to 3.99, 39.13% at 4.0 or above and 4.34% failing.

Why it matters here: A directly comparable case to the CheMet study: a purpose-built video game replacing lecture drill for a foundational, formula-heavy topic, evaluated with the same before-and-after design the Wits team is running on crystallography and phase transformations, and a reminder that a small in-house build, not a commercial engine, can move marks.

Martínez Villalobos and Ríos Herrera, Estudios Pedagógicos 45(3), 115-125 (2019), open access · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: The Multi-Material Marbles Game: measuring real marbles to build an Ashby chart, open source for any classroom (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Students measure mechanical loss coefficient, thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity and density on marbles made from different material families, then plot their own Material Property Chart and reason about materials selection. Pilot studies report high engagement and increased interest in materials science; the CAD files, rules, material cards and equipment list are open source.

Why it matters here: A tactile route into structure-property relationships, the very topic the Wits study names as a learning barrier, and a ready-made open-source kit the CheMet team could trial alongside its own games.

Barnsdale, Daugela, Galos, Hülse, Tyler and Yu, 2025 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition, Montreal; DOI 10.18260/1-2--56982 · Peer-reviewed conference paper, American Society for Engineering Education

entry.title: OU Analyse: weekly machine-learning risk scores for every distance student, and a decade of published evaluation (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
OU Analyse predicts each student's risk of failing the next assignment and updates the prediction weekly for tutors and student support teams, with the aim of improving retention across the Open University. The team has published on teachers' use and perceptions three years after implementation (LAK 2023), on co-creating an equality, diversity and inclusion dashboard to address awarding gaps (BJET 2024) and on a student-facing dashboard designed with students (LAK 2025, Journal of Learning Analytics 2025).

Why it matters here: A mature, evaluated system in a distance-learning setting close to much South African provision, with an open dataset the PASS models can be benchmarked against and a research track record on how teachers actually use predictions.

The Open University, OU Analyse (Knowledge Media Institute); Herodotou et al., Journal of Learning Analytics and LAK 2023 to 2025 · Institutional system with peer-reviewed evaluations

entry.title: Students write the questions, the faculty prints the board: a materials-science board game across three engineering degrees (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A Party-and-Co style board game, its hexagonal board drawn from the graphene lattice, was built from more than 90 tests per category written by first-year mechanical engineering students and reviewed by staff, then played in Materials Science and Engineering (94 students), Microstructure and Phase Transformations (60) and Optical and Magnetic Behaviour of Materials (60). Between 80% and 84% of students said the game helped them understand the course, and 62% to 81% that they retained more than with their usual methods; participation ran at 80% to 86%.

Why it matters here: Closest published cousin of the CheMet study: a board game on phase transformations and microstructure, in the language of the students, with the survey-based evaluation the Wits team also plans. The students-as-authors step is worth borrowing for the co-design workshops.

Riquelme, de Prado, Bonache, Rams, Sánchez, Torres, Escalera Rodriguez, Rodrigo and Muñoz, Education Sciences 14(10), 1054 (2024), open access · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Materials Battleships and Materials Taboo: a gamified first-year materials course for more than 1,200 learners (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Two adapted board games, Materials Battleships and Materials Taboo, plus custom virtual emulators of material behaviour were run for over 1,200 first-year engineering learners in person and online. Surveys reported that gamification stimulated interest in materials science and the motivation to take part, with more students saying they would pursue materials courses later.

Why it matters here: Scale evidence for the Wits study: the same mix of table games and digital play the CheMet project proposes, tested on a large first-year cohort where retention of foundational concepts is the problem.

Earle, DiCecco, Binkley, Arshad, Lucentini, Tembrevilla and Yu, 2023 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition · Peer-reviewed conference paper, American Society for Engineering Education

entry.title: Siyaphumelela: a national data-for-student-success network reaching 80% of South Africa's public university students (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Launched in 2014, Siyaphumelela works with post-school institutions to use data to improve access, retention, progression, graduation and work-readiness. It reports 20 partner universities, 80% of public university students reached, more than 1,500 university staff trained and R338 million invested, with an annual national conference and a focus on eliminating performance gaps by race, gender and socio-economic status.

Why it matters here: The South African ecosystem PASS sits inside: the institutions, staff and data practices already built through Siyaphumelela are the natural partners and audience for the Wits models and interventions, and the network's conference is a dissemination route.

Siyaphumelela, led by Saide in partnership with The Kresge Foundation (initiative site) · National initiative, funder-backed

entry.title: GPS Advising: more than 800 alerts, every undergraduate tracked daily, advisers who act the same week (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Georgia State runs predictive analytics over all undergraduates with a system of more than 800 alerts; when an alert fires, an adviser intervenes. The system went live in August 2012 and in one recent academic year generated more than 55,000 adviser-student meetings about specific alerts. Since 2012 first-year fall-to-spring retention has risen by five percentage points and graduating seniors take fewer excess courses.

Why it matters here: The best-known working model of what PASS proposes: prediction is only half the design; the other half is a person with time to act on each alert. Georgia State's alert-to-adviser loop is the pattern to test with Wits Business Intelligence Services and the School's advisers.

Georgia State University, Student Success Initiatives (institutional page) · Institutional programme page
